questions.question: What was the first AI Scientist v2 result that crossed a peer-review threshold?
options: A generated paper was published in Nature
A generated paper passed peer review at an ICLR 2025 workshop
A generated paper won best paper at NeurIPS 2025
A generated paper was accepted to a top-10 conference as a main track paper
questions.explanation: One AI Scientist v2-generated paper passed peer review at an ICLR 2025 workshop. The authors disclosed the paper's origin to the program committee. This is a proof of concept, not a reliability claim: workshop papers are a lower bar than main-conference papers.

questions.question: According to Beel et al.'s independent evaluation, what fraction of AI Scientist v2 experiments failed from coding errors?
options: About 10%
About 25%
About 42%
About 65%
questions.explanation: Beel et al. found 42% of experiments failed from coding errors (bad imports, shape mismatches, undefined variables). The retry loop caught some but not all of these failures.

questions.question: What is 'polish masking' as identified by Beel et al.'s evaluation of AI Scientist v2?
options: The model refusing to generate figures for failed experiments
Publication-grade visuals produced by the vision-language critique masking underlying experimental weaknesses
A post-processing step that removes politically sensitive content from papers
The model adding excessive citations to make papers look more credible
questions.explanation: AI Scientist v2's vision-language figure critique produced publication-grade visuals, masking underlying experimental weaknesses. This is the most important finding: a system producing convincing outputs without doing convincing research is more dangerous than one that fails obviously.

questions.question: What is the key architectural difference between AI Scientist v1 and v2?
options: v2 uses a larger base model while v1 used GPT-3
v1 used human-authored templates while v2 uses agentic tree search with a VLM figure critique loop
v2 can only run for one hour while v1 had no time limit
v1 submitted papers automatically while v2 requires human approval
questions.explanation: AI Scientist v1 required human-authored templates that the LLM filled in. v2 removes the template requirement by using agentic tree search over a space of hypotheses, with a vision-language model critique loop that rewrites figures for clarity.

questions.question: Why does AI Scientist v2 require stronger sandbox isolation than AlphaEvolve?
options: Because research papers are larger files than code programs
Because v2 runs open-ended code with open-ended goals, while AlphaEvolve has a tight, deterministic evaluator
Because research agents require internet access to fetch papers
Because v2 needs more compute than AlphaEvolve can safely allocate
questions.explanation: AlphaEvolve's sandbox story is easier because its evaluator is tight and machine-checkable. AI Scientist v2 runs open-ended code with open-ended goals, creating paths to data exfiltration, compute waste, and process spawning. Sakana's own docs recommend Docker isolation minimum, with seccomp or gVisor preferred.

questions.question: What does the 'novelty mislabeling' failure mode mean in AI Scientist v2?
options: The system assigns incorrect author names to generated papers
The literature-retrieval step frequently classifies established concepts as novel, the research equivalent of hallucination
The system generates ideas that are too novel to be understood by reviewers
The system fails to label figures with correct captions
questions.explanation: Beel et al. found the literature-retrieval step frequently flagged established concepts as novel. This is the research equivalent of hallucination: the system claims originality it cannot support.
